corrected_value.title: The beneficial and detrimental effects of major depression on intuitive decision-making.

decisions.location: The Current Study, lines 198-202; References, lines 1098-1100
decisions.quote:
The first hypothesis (H1) refers to the replica‐
bility of recently found intuition deficits in depression (Remmers et al., 2015; Remmers et
al., 2017). We hypothesized that patients with an acute episode of major depression are
less able to intuitively discriminate semantic coherence from semantic incoherence in the
JSCT than healthy controls.
decisions.reason: Prior adjudication and state files are absent for this work. In The Current Study (lines 198-202), Hypothesis 1 (H1) explicitly tests the replicability of intuition deficits in depression reported by both Remmers et al. (2015) and Remmers et al. (2017) by comparing semantic coherence discrimination in the JSCT between patients with acute major depression and healthy controls. The reference list (lines 1098-1100) and Crossref metadata identify Remmers et al. (2017) as a distinct empirical study published in Cognition and Emotion (DOI: 10.1080/02699931.2016.1154817, with coauthor Buxton), whereas the sole shipped row (2485, DOI: 10.1111/bjc.12069) is the 2014/2015 British Journal of Clinical Psychology study (sibling target 0).

corrected_value.title: The architecture of intuition: Fluency and affect determine intuitive judgments of semantic and visual coherence and judgments of grammaticality in artificial grammar learning.

decisions.location: The Current Study, lines 224-229; Discussion, lines 732-736; References, lines 1152-1155
decisions.quote:
The third hypothesis (H3a) was that the positive valence of stimuli influences seman‐

tic coherence judgments in patients with depression. Building up on basic research
(Topolinski & Strack, 2009a; Experiment 8) showing that healthy subjects are more
likely to judge triads to be coherent that consist of positive as compared to negative
words, we expected that this effect would also emerge for depressed patients.
decisions.reason: Prior adjudication and state files are absent for this work. The paper explicitly retests two empirical findings from Topolinski and Strack (2009a): the figure-ground contrast processing fluency manipulation from Experiment 1 (H2a/H2b; Appendix A lines 1215-1217; Appendix B lines 1269-1273; Discussion lines 732-736) and the positive versus negative word-triad valence manipulation on semantic coherence judgments from Experiment 8 (H3a/H3b; lines 224-235; Appendix B lines 1292-1297). The reference list (lines 1152-1155) identifies Topolinski & Strack (2009a) in Journal of Experimental Psychology: General (DOI: 10.1037/a0014678), which is completely absent from the sole shipped row (2485, DOI: 10.1111/bjc.12069).

corrected_value.title: The analysis of intuition: Processing fluency and affect in judgements of semantic coherence.

decisions.quote:
Results did not reveal any effect of our fluency manipulation, and thus our hypothe‐

ses regarding fluency (H2) were not supported. As such, the current study could not
replicate previous results that bolstered the fluency model proposed by Topolinski and
Strack (2009a, 2009b).
decisions.reason: Prior adjudication and state files are absent for this work. Using the JSCT fluency and valence blocks in depressed and healthy participants, the authors explicitly state in the Discussion (lines 732-736) that their fluency manipulation failed to replicate previous results bolstering the fluency model of Topolinski and Strack (2009a, 2009b), and further compare their valence-by-coherence accuracy interaction against the phasic positive affect finding of Topolinski and Strack (2009b) (lines 783-792). The reference list (lines 1157-1160) identifies Topolinski & Strack (2009b) in Cognition and Emotion (DOI: 10.1080/02699930802420745), which is distinct from both Topolinski & Strack (2009a) and the sole shipped row (2485, DOI: 10.1111/bjc.12069).

decisions.quote: Previous research has found that negative-valence appeals relating to the self (Don't be a cheater) are more effective at reducing unethical behaviour than appeals relating to behaviour (Don't cheat). We aimed to replicate these findings and examine whether positive-valence appeals relating to the self (Be an honest person) and to behaviour (Answer honestly) could have a similar effect.
decisions.reason: Prior adjudication and state files are absent for this work. The supplied source text consists solely of an abstract that states the authors aimed to replicate 'Previous research' finding that negative-valence appeals relating to the self ('Don't be a cheater') are more effective at reducing unethical behaviour than appeals relating to behaviour ('Don't cheat'). Because the supplied text contains no in-text citation and no reference list, the blind target has empty identity fields and primary-source evidence cannot establish the original work's identity or resolve whether the unnamed target in the abstract is the exact same work as shipped row 598 (Bryan, Adams, & Monin, 2013, DOI: 10.1037/a0030655) or an additional cited original.

decisions.quote: A previous study demonstrated that preventing mirror errors in reading requires the inhibition of the mirror generalization process in expert adult readers (Borst et al., 2015). Using the same experimental paradigm, the current study aimed at replicating this result in school-aged children.
decisions.reason: Prior adjudication and state files are absent for this work. The abstract states that the current study aimed to replicate in school-aged children a previous study in expert adult readers (cited as 'Borst et al., 2015') using the same negative-priming paradigm (primes with mirror letters b/d vs. non-mirror letters f/t followed by probes with animals facing opposite directions). Crossref bibliography metadata confirms that shipped row 2136 (Borst, Ahr, Roell, & Houdé, DOI: 10.3758/s13423-014-0663-9, 'The cost of blocking the mirror generalization process in reading: evidence for the role of inhibitory control in discriminating letters with lateral mirror-image counterparts') was published online in May 2014 and in print in 2015 in Psychonomic Bulletin & Review, Vol. 22, Issue 1, pp. 228-234. Thus, the candidate target is the exact same original work already represented by shipped row 2136 under its online publication year (2014).

corrected_value.title: Horses (Equus caballus) select the greater of two quantities in small numerical contrasts

decisions.location: Introduction, lines 240-244; Discussion, lines 454-456; References, lines 1911-1930
decisions.reason: The prior adjudication rightly recognized Uller & Lewis (2009) as a missing row but had schema errors in corrected_value (using 'type' instead of 'record_type' and a non-default outcome). The paper explicitly states as its second aim (Introduction, lines 240-244) that it tests the robustness of horses' quantity discrimination performance reported by Uller and Lewis (2009) using a different methodological approach across the same numerical contrasts (1:2, 2:3, 4:6, plus additional pairs; lines 235, 300-310, Table 1), and directly contrasts its null discrimination results against Uller and Lewis (2009) in the Discussion (lines 454-456, 521-523). Reference 60 (lines 1911-1930) provides full citation details (Animal Cognition 12, 733-738, DOI: 10.1007/s10071-009-0225-0), and this target is absent from the sole shipped row (1111, Schmitt & Fischer, 2011, DOI: 10.1038/ncomms1262).
